title: What are Flink's three time semantics (event time = when it happened, processing time = system clock, ingestion time = when it entered the pipeline) and when do you use each?
shortTitle: What are Flink's three time semantics
keyPoints: Event time is the timestamp embedded in each record describing when the event actually occurred at its source.
Processing time is the wall-clock time of the machine running the operator at the moment it handles the record.
Ingestion time is the timestamp assigned by the Flink source operator when the record first enters the pipeline.
Event time gives deterministic, replayable, out-of-order-tolerant results through watermarks but needs more configuration.
Processing time gives the lowest latency and simplest setup but is non-deterministic and unsuitable for auditable results.
Event time is the correct default for any financial or audit workload where the business cares about when money moved.

s1_definition.oneliner: Event time is when the event happened, processing time is when the operator handled it, and ingestion time is when it entered Flink; event time is the correct default for auditable results.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Event time** – The timestamp embedded in each record describing when the event actually occurred at its source, such as the moment a card was swiped at the ATM.
- **Processing time** – The wall-clock time of the machine running the operator at the instant it handles the record, requiring no timestamp extraction or watermarks.
- **Ingestion time** – The timestamp assigned by the Flink source operator when the record first enters the pipeline, behaving like event time downstream but ignoring true source delays.
- **Watermarks** – Special markers that flow with the stream in event-time mode, declaring that all events up to a certain time have been seen, enabling windows to fire correctly despite out-of-order data.
- **Determinism** – Event time results are deterministic and replayable because grouping depends on the data, not on when or how fast you process it.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine Rajesh swipes his card at an ATM at exactly 10:00:00. Event time is the clock printed on the receipt at the ATM, the true moment it happened. Ingestion time is the time stamped by the National Bank of India's front-gate security the moment the transaction message walks through the bank's door. Processing time is whatever time the back-office clerk's wall clock shows when the clerk finally gets around to processing the slip. If the network was slow, all three can differ by minutes.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
  Three Time Semantics for a Transaction

  Real world        Flink Source         Flink Operator
  ──────────        ────────────         ──────────────
  ATM Swipe         Enters Pipeline      Processes Record
  10:00:00          10:00:02             10:00:05
     │                  │                    │
     ▼                  ▼                    ▼
  Event Time        Ingestion Time       Processing Time
  (in the record)   (at source entry)    (operator clock)


  Watermark-Driven Window Firing (Event Time)

  Events:   [10:00:03] [10:00:01] [10:00:07] [10:00:05]
               │          │          │          │
               ▼          ▼          ▼          ▼
  Stream:  ──▶ E1 ──▶ E2 ──▶ E3 ──▶ E4 ──▶ ...

  Watermarks (5s allowed lateness):
  After E1: W(09:59:58)
  After E3: W(10:00:02)
  After En: W(10:00:55) ──▶ Window [10:00-10:01) FIRES


  Processing Time vs Event Time Results

  Same data, replayed at different times:

  Event Time:       Window [10:00] = Rs125,000  (always)
  Processing Time:  Window [10:00] = Rs125,000  (first run)
                    Window [11:00] = Rs125,000  (replay at 11:00)
                    Results differ by window placement!
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Flink gives you three ways to reason about time, and picking the right one is one of the most important decisions in a streaming job. Event time is the timestamp carried inside the record itself, describing when the event actually happened at its source. Processing time is the wall-clock time of the machine running the operator at the instant it handles the record. Ingestion time is the timestamp the source operator stamps the moment the record first enters Flink.

Event time is deterministic and replayable because the grouping depends only on the data, so reprocessing the same stream later gives identical results. But it needs watermarks to decide when a window is complete, and you must decide how long to wait for stragglers. Processing time has the lowest latency and needs no watermarks, but it is non-deterministic because the same records replayed at a different speed land in different windows. Ingestion time sits in between but is rarely the explicit choice today.

At the National Bank of India, our end-of-day settlement report absolutely had to use event time because it is reconciled against the card network by the business minute when money moved. During peak hours the queue backed up, so processing time would have placed transactions in the wrong minute and broken reconciliation. In parallel, our operations health dashboard used processing-time windows because it only answered how many transactions the servers were handling right now, and simplicity mattered more than source-true grouping.

The rule is simple: if the result must be correct, auditable, or replayable, use event time. If you only need a rough operational metric, processing time is fine.

Remember one sentence: Event time is when the event happened and gives deterministic replayable results; processing time is when the operator sees it and is fast but non-deterministic.
